The upcoming MacBook Ultra was never going to be cheap. Beyond its brand-new slim design, OLED display, and touch capabilities, it also has to absorb pricing pressures driven by rising memory costs. The latest reports suggest its production costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple has traditionally favored sourcing components from multiple suppliers to ensure a steady display supply and secure the best pricing, and had originally planned to continue this strategy with the MacBook Ultra. However, according to supply chain sources, Apple has decided to use only a single display supplier…

Apple has three display partners: Samsung, LG, and BOE. BOE has so far primarily supplied screens for Apple's lower-end products, while orders for high-end displays have consistently been shared between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature Apple's most sophisticated display to date, combining a two-stack tandem OLED structure with touch functionality on the large panels required for a laptop — no easy feat. According to the latest supply chain sources, Apple has decided to source panels solely from Samsung.

According to The Elec, LG has been unable to meet Apple's production standard requirements.

Apple requires large substrates for mass production, and Samsung Display has responded with its 8.6-generation OLED production line. LG Display is reportedly exploring the use of its existing 6-generation line. While 6-generation lines can produce laptop OLEDs, substrate efficiency and capacity fall short compared to 8.6-generation lines. Since early production volumes are clearly insufficient to support two suppliers, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as its sole supplier.

Given LG's limited production capacity, the logistics complexity of a dual-supplier setup clearly does not make sense. LG is not expected to supply screens for the flagship MacBook until 2029 at the earliest.

This situation clearly gives Samsung a stronger position in panel price negotiations, which is expected to further drive up Apple's production costs. Apple will likely pass the additional expenses on to consumers, similar to how it has handled rising memory costs.

Given that the MacBook Ultra may carry a staggering price tag, how interested are you in upgrading? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
